entries.title: White Sox polled on team's top first-half players, moments — and how far they'll go from here
entries.summary: <p>Before he got hurt May 29, there was zero question who was putting the “M” in MVP of the surprisingly competitive <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="_blank" >White Sox</a>: Japanese rookie <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/07/10/white-sox-activate-munetaka-murakami-from-injured-list-option-jacob-gonzalez-to-charlotte" target="_blank" >Munetaka Murakami</a>, only the third Sox player to slug 20 home runs pre-June, joining Frank Thomas (1994) and Jim Thome (2006).</p><p>Since then, the Sox have had several pairs of hands on the wheel, steering them into a first-place tie with the Guardians in the American League Central entering their final series before the All-Star break.</p><p>So, who is the team’s first-half MVP? Is it 20-homer <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/07/04/miguel-vargas-chicago-white-sox-all-star-game-third-baseman-joe-crede-colson-montgomery-davis-martin" target="_blank" >infielder Miguel Vargas</a>, who will represent the team at the All-Star Game in Philadelphia? Infielder Colson Montgomery, with his 23 bombs? Starting pitcher Davis Martin, who has held things down with nine wins and a team-high 3.0 WAR? Someone else?</p><p>The Sun-Times poked around Rate Field asking for top threes.</p><p>Center fielder Tristan Peters and pitchers Grant Taylor and Erik Fedde each had Vargas and Martin 1-2. But Peters went with Taylor third, Taylor with rookie left fielder Sam Antonacci and Fedde with Peters.</p><p>“Sam is my sleeper pick,” Taylor said. “He brings something different to the clubhouse.”</p><p>“We weren’t sure what we were going to get in center this year, and [Peters] has been an unbelievable asset,” Fedde said.</p><p>Infielder Chase Meidroth’s top three: Montgomery, Murakami and Vargas. Pitcher Noah Schultz’s: Martin, Montgomery and Vargas.</p><p>Injured pitcher Mike Vasil, the cheerleader-in-chief, had it Murakami, Vargas and Antonacci, whom he called a “complete motor in this lineup.”</p><p>Said longtime TV analyst Steve Stone, “It’s Davis Martin, Vargas and you probably go, because of the power numbers, with Colson Montgomery. However, honorable mention certainly goes to Sam Antonacci.”</p><p><b>THE first-half moment</b></p><p>We also asked which play, win or other occurrence belongs at the top of this team’s list so far.</p><p>Meidroth kept to a broad stroke — “just giving ourselves a chance in the second half” — while Taylor pointed to the Sox’ seven walk-off wins.</p><p>“It sets the standard for what we’re doing because we’re never out of a game,” Taylor said. “We always have the chance to fight back. Bottom nine, we’re coming to play.”</p><p>One of those walk-offs came on Braden Montgomery’s two-run homer in the 10th inning to beat the Braves 6-5 at Rate Field on June 9 in the outfielder’s very first big-league game.</p><p>“That was the play for me,” Schultz said. “A guy gets called up and makes an immediate impact like that? Such a huge deal and really brought the team together.”</p><p>Peters and Fedde opted for the series win against the Cubs in mid-May. It ended with another two-run, 10th-inning blast, this one off the bat of catcher Edgar Quero to take the rubber match 9-8 in a wild scene on the South Side.</p><p>“I think that was one of the first times we all had belief that we were coming together well and playing good baseball,” Fedde said. “The whole hype of the city came out, and winning that series kind of cemented the thought that we were going to compete.”</p><p>Vasil threw a bit of a curveball, impressive for a guy recovering from Tommy John surgery.</p><p>“The easy one to say is the Quero walk-off against the Cubs, but I honestly think the biggest swing that took us in the right direction was the [Andrew] Benintendi home run [in the ninth inning on April 23] in Arizona. A three-run bomb in a tie game on the road? That was when it sort of turned for us for the year.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">EDGAR QUERO WALK-OFF HOME RUN THE WHITE SOX TAKE A SERIES FROM THE CUBS <a href="https://t.co/JPTSqeOHdP">pic.twitter.com/JPTSqeOHdP</a></p>— Talkin' Baseball (@TalkinBaseball_) <a href="https://x.com/TalkinBaseball_/status/2056125478595891627?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">May 17, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p><b>What happens from here?</b></p><p>When Murakami finally re-entered the lineup Friday, his hamstring trouble hopefully behind him, it felt almost like a major trade-deadline acquisition. Of course, it wasn’t one, and general manager Chris Getz soon will be on the clock to show how willing the Sox are to improve their roster from outside the organization.</p><p>Stone — who predicted on Opening Day the Sox would be much better than the 66 or 67 wins most analytics models projected for them — isn’t offering a second-half forecast this far out from the August 3 deadline.</p><p>“I don’t think there is any way Chris Getz wants to break up a farm system that he worked so hard to put together,” Stone said, “but it’s probably no secret they could use a starting pitcher [and] maybe another arm for the bullpen.”</p><p>The Guardians, Twins and Tigers all could be in play for the division title. A wild-card spot could be there for the grabbing in an AL with only two teams — the Rays and the Yankees — well clear of .500.</p><p>How are Sox players sizing up their chances?</p><p>“I easily see the talent of this team going into the playoffs,” Meidroth said. “At this point, it’s up to us.”</p><p>“We can win our division,” Peters said. “There’s no doubt in my mind.”</p><p>According to Fedde, anything less than a division title would be a “disappointment.” Sox fans who have witnessed three straight 100-plus-loss seasons might be more inclined to welcome any old postseason berth.</p><p>A couple of pitchers stuck their necks out even further.</p><p>“With Mune back, I think we’re going to play similar or better ball as we go forward, continue to build on what we’ve gone and grow and get better, and then we want to be playing deep into October,” Taylor said. “That’s the goals I have and what I expect from this team.”</p><p>Schultz put it all the way out there.</p><p>“Win the division, host playoff games, win the World Series,” he said. “If you’re not shooting for that, then you’re not playing the right sport.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/07/10/white-sox-activate-munetaka-murakami-from-injured-list-option-jacob-gonzalez-to-charlotte" >White Sox activate Munetaka Murakami from injured list, option Jacob Gonzalez to Charlotte</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/07/04/miguel-vargas-chicago-white-sox-all-star-game-third-baseman-joe-crede-colson-montgomery-davis-martin" target="_blank" >Miguel Vargas becomes White Sox’ first All-Star third baseman since Joe Crede in 2008</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Court monitor dings city for lacking a single compliant accessible crosswalk signal for impaired pedestrians
entries.summary: <p>One year after a federal judge ordered Chicago to install more accessible crosswalk signals for impaired pedestrians, a court-appointed monitor found the city has met the minimum requirements by installing 78 new signals.</p><p>But the monitor, in its <a class="Link" href="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/d3/e7/21bd91c14354aaf73233c7276cd6/pedestrian-crossing-monitor-report.pdf" target="_blank" >first-year report</a> published July 1, also found that none of Chicago's accessible signals — with their distinctive audible beeping — are compliant with federal standards.</p><p>"They're usable. But they're not as effective as they can and should be," says Rachel M. Weisberg, directing attorney at Disability Rights Advocates, which filed the original lawsuit in 2019 that led to court-appointed monitor Michael G. Shaw being named in June 2025.</p><p>The signals, when pressed, beep when it's safe to cross for blind and vision-impaired pedestrians. The buttons also vibrate to alert hearing-impaired pedestrians of a signal change.</p><p>The standards for the crosswalks, called accessible pedestrian signals, are determined by the U.S. Department of Transportation's Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices. The manual sets the technical specifications from everything from the height of button placement to the signal's distance from the curb, Weisberg said.</p><p>Besides failing the technical requirements, the monitor found that many devices were not functioning properly or required maintenance.</p><p>The city has work to do on that end, Weisberg said. But the city has made substantial progress at identifying and constructing accessible signals at crosswalks across the city.</p><p>In the first year under court supervision, the monitor found:<br></p><ul class="rte2-style-ul" id="rte-5310e822-7c79-11f1-9253-cbff6d5e8685"><li>The city installed 78 accessible pedestrian signals, eight more than what the court required. The requirements ramp up in the coming years. The city is required to build signals at 110 intersections in the second year of the judge's remedial order.</li><li>The city now has accessible signals at 165 intersections — only 6.5% of the city's 2,800 total intersections.</li><li>The Chicago Department of Transportation "demonstrated exemplary efforts" in following the judge's order, and has drafted an accessible pedestrian signal policy and has built several accessible signals at intersections requested by the public.</li></ul><p>The spokesperson for the Transportation Department, which oversees the installation of accessible signals, did not immediately have a comment on the monitor's report, but pointed to a June <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicago.gov/city/en/depts/cdot/provdrs/traffic_signals_andstreetlights/news/2026/june/city-of-chicago-expands-accessible-pedestrian-signals-citywide--.html" target="_blank" >news release</a> about the new accessible signals.</p><p>Since 2019, the city has built accessible signals at all intersection reconstruction projects, the release states. </p><p>"This significant expansion of Accessible Pedestrian Signals is about making our streets more inclusive and ensuring residents who are blind or have low vision can travel more independently in every neighborhood," Mayor Brandon Johnson was quoted as saying in the release. His office did not immediately reply to a request for comment.</p><p>The city has website, <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagoaps.org/" target="_blank" >chicagoaps.org/</a>, with a map of Chicago's accessible intersections. The site also has a form for residents to request new accessible signals.</p><p>U.S. District Judge LaShona Hunt <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2025/03/19/blind-visually-impaired-pedestrian-crossing-intersections-judge-order-installation" target="_blank" >placed the city under a remedial order</a> in March 2025, aiming to resolve a lawsuit filed six years ago by the American Council of the Blind of Metropolitan Chicago.</p><p>The lawsuit accused the city of violating the Americans for Disabilities Act by failing to build signalized street intersections with accessible pedestrian signals.</p><p>The order mandates the city to install the devices at at least 71% of signaled intersections by the end of 2035, and five additional years to hit the 100% mark.</p><p>For years, Chicago officials talked about launching pilot programs to address the scarcity of accessible signals, Weisberg said. She's heartened to see the city finally taking the issue seriously.</p><p>Other cities have been slow to adopt accessible signals. New York City lost a lawsuit in 2022 that claimed it violated the Americans for Disabilities Act because it lacked accessible signals at 95% of its intersections. That city is now under a similar court order.</p><p>Disability Rights Advocates <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2025/09/10/chicago-pedestrian-ways-violate-ada-requirements-lawsuit-alleges" target="_blank" >filed another lawsuit</a> last year alleging the city has not done enough to improve the accessibility of its sidewalks and curbs.</p><p>With time, Chicago could become a model for accessible infrastructure, Weisberg said.</p><p>"The hope is that Chicago can be a leader to support the blind and vision-impaired community," she said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe src="https://docs.google.com/viewer?embedded=true&url=https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/d3/e7/21bd91c14354aaf73233c7276cd6/pedestrian-crossing-monitor-report.pdf"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p></p>

entries.title: 2 killed in minivan-semitruck crash in Hegewisch
entries.summary: <p>Two people inside a minivan died when they rear-ended a semitruck Friday morning in the Far South Side's Hegewisch neighborhood, police said.</p><p>The semi was eastbound in the 2700 block of East 130th Street about 9:15 a.m., trying to make a left turn when a Dodge Grand Caravan, also eastbound, rear-ended the semi, police said. </p><p>The two people in the minivan, identified only as male, were taken to the University of Chicago Medical Center where they were pronounced dead, police said. </p><p>No one else was hurt. </p><p>The police major accidents investigation unit is probing the wreck. <br></p>

entries.title: Los arrestos de ICE han aumentado en Chicago, pero con tácticas menos llamativas que el otoño pasado
entries.summary: <p>La aplicación federal de la ley de inmigración se ha intensificado en Chicago en las últimas semanas, pero las tácticas de la administración de Trump han sido mucho menos publicitadas que durante el auge de su campaña de deportación el otoño pasado, dicen grupos legales y defensores de la inmigración.</p><p>La semana pasada, al menos 20 personas fueron arrestadas por el Servicio de Inmigración y Control de Aduanas (ICE) en Chicago, y otras 17 personas han sido detenidas esta semana hasta ahora, según informes de grupos de respuesta rápida que documentan los arrestos.</p><p>Esos números parecen ser un aumento con respecto a los meses recientes, dijo Marcela Rodríguez, copresidenta de la Agenda Latina de Illinois y miembro del grupo sin fines de lucro Enlace Chicago.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-c30000" name="module-c30000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>El lado suroeste, particularmente los vecindarios de Back of the Yards, Brighton Park y Gage Park, han sido los más afectados recientemente, dijeron los grupos legales.</p><p>La actividad aumentada de ICE en Chicago ocurre en medio de una campaña de deportación escalada por la administración de Trump en todo el país.</p><p>El martes, un oficial de ICE le disparó y mató a un hombre en Houston durante un intento de detención de tráfico.</p><p>Durante el período de cinco días a finales de junio, ICE arrestó a más de 10,000 personas. Las cifras indican que, aunque la administración ya no se concentra en esfuerzos llamativos en ciudades individuales, los arrestos continúan y están en aumento.</p><p>“Estos números representan más que estadísticas”, dijo Rodríguez el jueves en una conferencia de prensa en Back of the Yards con numerosos líderes de defensa de inmigrantes. “Representan a padres, hijos, trabajadores, vecinos, propietarios de negocios pequeños y miembros de nuestra comunidad que merecen dignidad, justicia y debido proceso”.</p><p>Los grupos legales dijeron que esos números también pueden subestimar la cantidad real de arrestos porque los agentes federales de inmigración han operado de manera más discreta en comparación con el otoño pasado, cuando caravanas de agentes vestidos con uniformes militares recorrían las calles, utilizaban helicópteros, filmaban arrestos y se jactaban de ellos en las redes sociales.</p><p>Aún así, muchos de los arrestos recientes han ocurrido en espacios públicos, como cortes, escuelas y supermercados.</p><p>La vasta mayoría de los recientes detenidos en Chicago también no tienen antecedentes penales, dijo Berto Aguayo, abogado y copresidente de políticas del Consejo de Liderazgo Latino.</p><p>“A pesar de las afirmaciones de que el 'Operativo Midway Blitz' ha terminado, no es así”, dijo Aguayo. “Nuestras comunidades continúan sintiendo el impacto. Las familias siguen viviendo con las consecuencias y la litigación continúa hasta el día de hoy debido al daño continuo causado por este operativo”.</p><p>“Así que nuestro mensaje hoy sigue siendo el mismo: Si eres vulnerable, por favor toma precauciones y limita salir; conoce tus derechos, mantente informado; conéctate con organizaciones comunitarias de confianza y tus vecinos”.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-1d517b" name="image-1d517b"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/c8d4ad2/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1024x575+0+54/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ff9%2Fb3%2F2a2c49724a32a05f36f63e3e7399%2Fice-260710-5.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/7b8d295/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1024x575+0+54/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ff9%2Fb3%2F2a2c49724a32a05f36f63e3e7399%2Fice-260710-5.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/20b03f4/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1024x575+0+54/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ff9%2Fb3%2F2a2c49724a32a05f36f63e3e7399%2Fice-260710-5.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Berto Aguayo, copresidente del Consejo de Liderazgo Latino, habla con periodistas durante una conferencia de prensa el jueves para denunciar un aumento de la actividad de ICE en la zona. La conferencia se realizó en la intersección de 47th Street y Damen Avenue, en el barrio de Back of the Yards.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Tyler Pasciak LaRiviere/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>La operación menos ostentosa de ICE ha afectado a los residentes “de una buena y de una mala manera”, dijo Rodríguez.</p><p>“De una buena manera porque hay cierto alivio que se siente de alguna manera para algunas personas”, detalló Rodríguez. “Pero de una mala manera porque… me preocuparía que nos sintamos cómodos con el silencio, aunque en realidad no está realmente silencioso, simplemente no es tan visible como solía ser. Así que eso pone a las personas en peligro”.</p><p>En el último mes, el número de solicitudes de servicios legales de inmigración realizadas al Proyecto Resurrección ha aumentado casi el doble, de 900 consultas a más de 1,700, dijo el director ejecutivo de la organización, Raul Raymundo.</p><p>Otros grupos han visto el mismo aumento en las consultas.</p><p>En Enlace Chicago, las solicitudes de servicios han aumentado significativamente en las últimas semanas, aseguró Rodríguez.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure entries.title: Chicago murals: Albany Park artist draws inspiration from science

Avenue, she called experts at the Shedd Aquarium for insight on native Lake Michigan flora and fauna, and invasive critters, too.</p><p>The result is a massive spread in <a class="Link" Invasive sea lamprey adhere to the purple columns in the murals.</p><p>While realistic, Robbins also “wanted the piece to remain optimistic.” Colorful images that look like rainbow trees were inspired by viewing butterfly wings under a microscope, she says, and the lights of fireflies seem to flash underneath.</p><p>“That’s my main goal that I want viewers to take away from the artwork,” Robbins says. “I want them to be excited about learning about all these flora and fauna that make up this environment.”</p><p>Her murals represent second chances in a way, too. entries.title: White Sox activate Munetaka Murakami from injured list, option Jacob Gonzalez to Charlotte
entries.summary: <p>The White Sox officially activated Munetaka Murakami from the injured list Friday and optioned Jacob Gonzalez to Triple-A Charlotte. </p><p>Murakami, who played in two rehab games this week in Charlotte to complete his recovery from a strained right hamstring, will be in the lineup for the game tonight against the Athletics at Rate Field (6:40 p.m., CHSN, 1000-AM). A sellout crowd is expected.</p><p>“He feels good. He’s ready to go,” manager Will Venable said Thursday when he announced that Murakami would be activated after a successful rehab assignment. “He was challenged running the bases. Defensively, had a really long game yesterday of nine innings. So [we] feel good about the work; he recovered well today. So he’s ready to go.”</p><p>Murakami, who still ranks second on the team with 20 home runs, went 2-for-7 with an RBI double, a walk and two strikeouts at Charlotte. He played five innings at first base Tuesday and nine innings Wednesday. The Sox might give Murakami some time at designated hitter as he returns to game-playing shape.</p><p>“There’ll be a lot of communication on where he’s at,” Venable said. “This ramp-up and this rehab was obviously very quick. So we want to be mindful of where he’s at day to day.”</p><p>Murakami, 26, has missed the last 35 games, in which the Sox held their own with a record of 17-18. Before suffering the injury running to first base May 30, Murakami was slashing .240/.378/.560 with four doubles, 41 RBI, 44 walks and 43 runs scored in 57 games. His 20 homers are tied for seventh in the American League.</p><p>The Sox called up Gonzalez, 24, the day after Murakami's injury — which he suffered six weeks ago today — and put him through a crash course at first base. After some early mental mistakes, Gonzalez caught on and capably handled the position. He had hoped that his ability to play everywhere else on the infield — he has been a shortstop for most of his career — would keep him with the Sox when Murakami returned.</p><p>“We all know I can play all the positions,” he told the Sun-Times on Thursday. “Obviously, I came up here to fill the first-baseman role while he was hurt. I think it was good I showed that I can play there." </p><p>Gonzalez slashed .244/.323/.360 with four doubles, two home runs, 17 RBI and 11 runs scored in 30 games with the Sox in his first major-league season.</p><p>Murakami is returning at a time the Sox' offense is sputtering. In losing all three games to the Red Sox this week, the White Sox scored two runs with 15 hits — all singles — in 27 innings and struck out 25 times.</p><p>“Obviously, he’s a presence in the lineup,” designated hitter Andrew Benintendi said. “He’ll bring energy. Seems like the vibe in here is kind of down right now. But I’m sure seeing him will spark it back up.”</p><p>“It’s going to be a great jolt,” Venable said. “That’s real. We understand the impact that he makes on the field and in the clubhouse. Really excited about it.”</p><div class="PageListL" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" data-show-loadmore="true" ><a class="AnchorLink" entries.title: Jornalero de Chicago gana acuerdo de $9 millones por confesión forzada y condena errónea
entries.summary: <p>Los contribuyentes de Chicago gastarán $9 millones para compensar a un hombre que pasó 17 años en prisión después de haber sido golpeado y coaccionado, cuando era adolescente, para firmar una confesión por un asesinato que no cometió.</p><p>El último en una serie aparentemente interminable de acuerdos por condenas erróneas vinculadas a mala conducta de los oficiales de la Policía de Chicago —$131.5 millones sólo en los primeros seis meses, según un análisis de WTTW— va destinado a Alberto Ochoa.</p><p>Ochoa era un jornalero de 17 años que había llegado a Chicago desde México menos de un año antes, cuando fue arrestado y acusado del asesinato de Marilu Sochu en diciembre de 2002, después de haber sido identificado falsamente por un conocido miembro de la pandilla Latin Kings.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-aa0000" name="module-aa0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Los oficiales de la Policía de Chicago, liderados por José “Pepe” López, fueron acusados de obligar a uno de varios miembros de los Latin Kings arrestados por un robo esa misma noche, para que identificara a Ochoa como el asesino de la novia de un miembro de una pandilla rival.</p><p>Se les prometió a los miembros de la pandilla que serían liberados de inmediato si identificaban al tirador.</p><p>Ochoa conocía y trabajaba con uno de los miembros de los Latin Kings, quien había ido al apartamento de Ochoa en La Villita la noche del asesinato para cobrar dinero prestado.</p><p>Pero él no era miembro de la pandilla y no tuvo ningún papel en el robo ni en el asesinato de la joven. Ochoa pasó la noche del asesinato viendo películas y tomando cerveza en casa.</p><p>La abogada Jennifer Bonjean, que representó a Ochoa, dijo que la mala conducta policial que culminó en la condena errónea de su cliente sigue un patrón familiar y preocupante.</p><p>Después de ser implicado falsamente por ese miembro de los Latin Kings y arrestado por la policía, Bonjean dijo que Ochoa fue brutalmente abusado y engañado para que firmara su nombre en una confesión “fabricada” redactada sólo en inglés.</p><p>“Lo estranguló y le metió el pulgar profundamente en el hueco del cuello… donde está el esófago. Durante meses, tuvo que recibir tratamiento médico en el [hospital] Cermak. Fue golpeado a puños... Y fue golpeado en los genitales”, dijo Bonjean.</p><p>Antes de firmar la confesión inventada redactada en inglés, Bonjean dijo que Ochoa solicitó hacer una declaración grabada en video en su lugar. La solicitud fue denegada, aunque el equipo de grabación de video estaba disponible, agregó.</p><p>“Mi cliente terminó firmando —o realmente imprimiendo— su nombre en una declaración manuscrita que no pudo leer y que no escribió... implicándose en este crimen. Había declaraciones allí que estaban completamente fabricadas, pero él no estaba al tanto porque no podía leerla”, dijo Bonjean el jueves.</p><p>“Es absolutamente escandaloso que tuvieras al detective principal de un caso actuando como intérprete y detective principal con una persona que no habla inglés. No podemos vivir en un mundo donde la gente firme… declaraciones que no pueden leer. Eso fue un acto escandaloso de mala conducta”, aseguró.</p><p>“López, este detective que habla español que era la única persona con la que se comunicaba, dijo: 'Sólo necesitamos que hagas una declaración y luego podrás irte a casa'. El detective escribió la declaración en inglés, aunque había disponibilidad para grabación de video, y mi cliente solicitó que su declaración fuera grabada en video. Se le negó. Así que, esencialmente, firmó una declaración donde se implicaba a sí mismo y que no podía leer. Y hubo aspectos de la misma que el detective López había fabricado”.</p><p>Ochoa, que ahora trabaja como conductor de camión, fue liberado de prisión en octubre de 2019. Se le otorgó un certificado de inocencia en noviembre de 2023.</p><p>Se pedirá al Comité de Finanzas del Concejo Municipal que apruebe el acuerdo de $9 millones durante la reunión del lunes.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (AI) y editado por </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a><br></p>

entries.title: Fifth heat-related death recorded in Chicago area
entries.summary: <p>The death of a 47-year-old Greater Grand Crossing neighborhood woman marks the fifth person to die, at least in part, due to the heat since July 1 in the Chicago area, officials said Friday. </p><p>An autopsy Friday determined the primary cause of Stephanie Rodriguez's death was complications from heat stroke, according to the Cook County medical examiner's office. A secondary cause was schizophrenia. </p><p>Rodriguez, of the 700 Block of East 76th Street, suffered the injuries at West 53rd Street and South Halsted Street in the Back of the Yards neighborhood, according to the medical examiner's office. Rodriguez was pronounced dead at 3:52 a.m. Thursday at the University of Chicago Medical Center.</p><p>Four other people have died since July 1, at least in part, due to the heat. </p><p>On July 3rd, a 71-year-old Barbara Whigham and 57-year-old Mike Rodriguez died, officials said. </p><p>Whigham was found unresponsive inside a residence in the 1000 block of West 70th Street in Englewood, and while her primary cause of death was heart disease, contributing causes of death were asthma, obesity and heat stress, according to the medical examiner's office. </p><p>Rodriguez, who was found unresponsive in a home in the 3200 block of South Archer Avenue in the McKinley Park neighborhood, died primarily of heart disease, with contributing factors being diabetes and heat stress, the medical examiner's office said. </p><p>On July 2, David Gonzalez, 44, was found unresponsive in a residence in the 2700 block of West 68th Street in Chicago Lawn by officers responding to a death investigation. Gonzalez was pronounced dead on July 4, and an autopsy determined the death was caused primarily by heat stroke. Contributing causes of his death were listed as heart disease, diabetes and obesity. </p><p>On July 1, Daniel Machnikowski, 69, died after being found at his home in the 1200 block of Darrow Street in north suburban Evanston. Machnikowski died primarily of heart disease, with heat stress listed as a secondary cause, the medical examiner's office said. </p><p>All five deaths come after <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/06/29/heat-wave-chicago-area-city-services" target="_blank" >health officials have warned</a> that prolonged periods of extreme heat can be especially dangerous for older adults, people with chronic medical conditions and those without reliable access to air conditioning.</p><p>Chicago currently has <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2026/06/30/chicago-heat-wave-extreme-weather-brandon-johnson-health-south-side-west-side" target="_blank" >287 citywide cooling facilities available</a> for residents seeking relief, including all 22 police districts, community service centers, Chicago Public Libraries, Chicago Park Districts, and senior centers, according to an earlier statement from the Mayor Brandon Johnson's office. </p><p>All six Community Service Centers will be open for cooling during standard operating hours of 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. Tuesday through Thursday, with the Garfield Community Service Center, 10 S. Kedzie Ave., extending cooling hours until 8 p.m. through Thursday. Garfield will also be open 9 a.m. to 8 p.m. on Friday, July 3, the mayor said in the statement.<br></p>

entries.title: Bears sign third-round pick Sam Roush
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" >Bears</a> signed third round draft pick Sam Roush to his rookie contract on Friday, about two weeks before the start of training camp.</p><p>The Bears have now agreed to deals with all of their draft picks.</p><p>The former Stanford tight end was allowed to participate during the team's off-season program, despite not having a signed contract. He could not have reported to training camp without one, though. </p><p>He and other third round draft picks we're negotiating for certain guarantees, though their salary is set by the collective bargaining agreement.</p><p>He is expected to serve as the Bears' third tight end behind standouts Colston Loveland and Cole Kmet. Coach Ben Johnson is among the league leaders in using multiple tight ends.</p><p>The Bears will report to training camp as a full team at the end of the month, though rookies and quarterbacks will show up a few days earlier.. </p><bsp-list-loadmore class="PageListH" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" data-show-loadmore="true" ><a entries.title: Jueza determina que el fiscal federal de Chicago violó su orden de secreto en caso de Tren de Aragua
entries.summary: <p>Cuando comenzó la audiencia, la jueza magistrada Laura McNally le dijo al principal fiscal federal de Chicago, “Agradecería si pudiera acercarse”.</p><p>Más de una semana antes, el fiscal federal Andrew Boutros viajó a Washington para una conferencia de prensa el 1 de julio para anunciar cargos criminales contra tres supuestos miembros de la pandilla Tren de Aragua, junto con el fiscal general interino Todd Blanche y el director del FBI Kash Patel.</p><p>Pero el jueves, Boutros se encontró siendo llamado por la jueza al frente de una de las salas de la corte más grandes de la Corte Federal Dirksen, abarrotada de espectadores se había reunido detrás de él. Durante casi media hora, estuvo de pie y escuchó a McNally decir que hubo una “clara” violación de su orden que sellaba el mismo caso que Boutros había ido a Washington a anunciar.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-300000" name="module-300000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>McNally no levantó ese sello hasta el 2 de julio, el día después de la conferencia de prensa. Y aunque dijo que su orden “no fue respetada por el Departamento de Justicia”, rechazó cualquier indicación de que la responsabilidad recayera en los fiscales de base.</p><p>“Lo que sé”, le dijo McNally a Boutros, “es que su declaración reconoce que estaba al tanto, cuando fue allí, de que había una orden de sellado en vigor”.</p><p>La audiencia del jueves giró en torno a un caso que imputa cargos federales de conspiración de secuestro contra Josué Pacheco Torres, Kleiver Monasterio Briceño y Julián Pachano. Una denuncia penal hecha pública alega que son un grupo de nacionales venezolanos, involucrados con Tren de Aragua, que participaron en un complot para secuestrar y matar a un hombre cuyo cuerpo fue descubierto por la policía el 19 de mayo dentro de un edificio abandonado en Chicago.</p><p>McNally dijo que su orden era “inequívoca”. No consideró que la orden se hubiera violado por “ningún propósito nefasto”. Sin embargo, no ordenó ninguna sanción. “También encuentro y concluyo —gracias a Dios— que no hubo daño concreto como resultado”, dijo.</p><p>Boutros le dijo a McNally que tomó sus comentarios “muy en serio”. Dijo que sus "intenciones eran cumplir con la orden”. Y le dijo a la jueza, “respeto sus conclusiones”.</p><p>La audiencia completa duró 40 minutos, incluidos los comentarios de Boutros.</p><p>Aunque pudo parecer anticlimático, la audiencia fue un momento extraordinario dentro de la corte Dirksen, donde la oficina de Boutros está en medio de una crisis de credibilidad distinta a la enfrentada por sus recientes predecesores. Es la segunda vez en siete semanas que un juez ha reprendido en persona al principal funcionario federal de la ley en el norte de Illinois.</p><p>La primera reprimenda ocurrió el 21 de mayo, después de que Boutros desestimó permanentemente los cargos contra un grupo de manifestantes del Operativo Midway Blitz conocidos como los “Broadview Six” debido a revelaciones de mala conducta por parte de su personal.</p><p>La jueza de distrito April Perry le dijo “está significativamente restándole valor a su mea culpa aquí al mantenerse detrás de los cargos y continuar difamando a estos acusados en particular” después de que él dijera que la conducta de ellos era “inaceptable en una sociedad civilizada”.</p><p>Desde entonces, han surgido numerosas controversias. Pero la más reciente, que llevó a la audiencia ante McNally, involucra a altos funcionarios del Departamento de Justicia. McNally dijo el jueves que también estaba preocupada por los comentarios hechos durante la conferencia de prensa por Blanche, a quien el presidente Donald Trump ha nominado para servir de manera permanente como el principal funcionario de aplicación de la ley del país.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a Kennedy del Departamento de Justicia en Washington, D.C. El Departamento de Justicia realizó la rueda de prensa para tratar desarrollos recientes en la investigación de la pandilla Tren de Aragua. A Blanche lo acompañaron el fiscal para el Distrito Norte de Illinois, Andrew Boutros (izq.), y el director del FBI, Kash Patel (der.).</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anna Moneymaker/Getty</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>“Esta mañana en Chicago, las fuerzas del orden federales y locales acusaron a tres supuestos miembros del [Tren de Aragua] en una denuncia criminal, acusándolos del brutal asesinato de otra víctima”, dijo Blanche durante la conferencia de prensa del 1 de julio, refiriéndose a la pandilla venezolana que la administración de Trump ha atacado agresivamente.</p><p>McNally le dijo a Boutros el jueves, “eso es más de lo que permitimos en nuestro expediente aquí, esa declaración”.</p><p>También señaló que “se usaron fotos de esta denuncia bajo sello y se pusieron en una pantalla”.</p><p>Los funcionarios del Departamento de Justicia no respondieron a una solicitud de comentarios.</p><p>Boutros está <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/04/07/chicago-crime-justice-department-doj-boutros-trump-midway-blitz-corruption" target="_blank" >a 15 meses de su mandato</a> como el principal fiscal federal de Chicago. La entonces fiscal general Pam Bondi lo designó para el cargo en abril de 2025 de forma temporal. Los <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2025/07/25/chicagos-federal-judges-choose-andrew-boutros-as-top-prosecutor" target="_blank" >jueces federales de Chicago eligieron a Boutros</a> para continuar con el trabajo de manera más permanente ese verano.</p><p>La jueza principal de distrito Virginia Kendall se negó, a través de un portavoz, a comentar sobre los procedimientos del jueves, citando el código de conducta judicial.</p><p>Mientras Boutros experimentó un primer año complicado en el cargo, la controversia que lo rodeaba no alcanzó su punto más alto hasta que Perry descubrió aparente mala conducta por parte del personal de Boutros durante los procedimientos del gran jurado en el caso de los “Broadview Six”.</p><p>Boutros ha anunciado reformas “amplias” del gran jurado y una <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2026/06/26/mientras-la-fiscal-de-los-broadview-six-enfrenta-juicio-boutros-no-escapa-del-peso-que-hay-en-su-oficina" target="_blank" >revisión de casi 20 años</a> del trabajo del veterano fiscal en el centro de ese escándalo.</p><p>Sin embargo, aún quedan preguntas sobre el papel que otros jugaron en el caso. Y nuevas controversias han surgido incluso en casos sin aparente conexión a los “Broadview Six”. Boutros y su equipo evitaron otras audiencias en las últimas semanas, pero Boutros no logró convencer a McNally de cancelar la audiencia del jueves.</p><p>McNally se unió al banco en noviembre de 2024 tras servir como socia de litigios en Loeb & Loeb LLP.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-291d05" name="image-291d05"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/30a322e/2147483647/strip/true/crop/972x546+0+248/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fbd%2F80%2F54bf9290436eb06895874b846853%2Fcomplaintimage1.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/c251215/2147483647/strip/true/crop/972x546+0+248/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fbd%2F80%2F54bf9290436eb06895874b846853%2Fcomplaintimage1.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/b904694/2147483647/strip/true/crop/972x546+0+248/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fbd%2F80%2F54bf9290436eb06895874b846853%2Fcomplaintimage1.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Una foto de la denuncia penal presentada contra Josué Pacheco Torres, Kleiver Monasterio Briceño y Julián Pachano. Las autoridades dicen que muestra (de izquierda a derecha) a la víctima del secuestro, a Torres y a un conspirador no identificado." srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/b904694/2147483647/strip/true/crop/972x546+0+248/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fbd%2F80%2F54bf9290436eb06895874b846853%2Fcomplaintimage1.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/7d1823b/2147483647/strip/true/crop/972x546+0+248/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fbd%2F80%2F54bf9290436eb06895874b846853%2Fcomplaintimage1.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/b904694/2147483647/strip/true/crop/972x546+0+248/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fbd%2F80%2F54bf9290436eb06895874b846853%2Fcomplaintimage1.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Una foto de la denuncia penal presentada contra Josué Pacheco Torres, Kleiver Monasterio Briceño y Julián Pachano. Las autoridades dicen que muestra (de izquierda a derecha) a la víctima del secuestro, a Torres y a un conspirador no identificado.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Corte del Distrito</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>McNally el 29 de junio ordenó que la denuncia y otros documentos en el caso fueran sellados “hasta el momento del arresto de todos los acusados en este caso o hasta nueva orden de la corte”. Dijo que la orden “no prohíbe a los funcionarios de las fuerzas del orden divulgar la denuncia, la declaración jurada y las órdenes de arresto según sea necesario para facilitar la aplicación de la ley penal”.</p><p>Pero el 30 de junio, Boutros dijo que fue invitado a la conferencia de prensa en Washington al día siguiente. Le dijo a la jueza el jueves que los funcionarios de las fuerzas del orden le aconsejaron esperar hasta la mañana del 1 de julio para intentar que la denuncia fuera hecha pública porque eso “sería el curso más seguro para proceder con la ejecución de las órdenes de arresto”.</p><p>Sin embargo, McNally dijo que los fiscales la llamaron a su oficina a las 10:05 a.m. del 1 de julio alegando que “necesitaban obtener una decisión dentro de los próximos 15 minutos”.</p><p>“Me dieron 15 minutos para considerar la moción,” le dijo McNally a Boutros el jueves. “… En ese momento, tenía otros asuntos urgentes, como su oficina bien sabía”.</p><p>Continuó diciendo “todo lo que hice” ese día “fueron audiencias que involucraban al Departamento de Justicia”.</p><p>Boutros le dijo, “la sincera esperanza era que, para cuando aterrizara en Washington, los tres acusados estuvieran bajo custodia. Y simplemente no funcionó así”.</p><p>Finalmente, dijo que “ya no tenía acceso a mis teléfonos” mientras se preparaba para aparecer en la conferencia de prensa.</p><p>“La última comunicación que vi de mi equipo fueron palabras en el sentido de: ‘Vamos a la oficina. Vamos a la oficina a ocuparnos de esto.’ Eso es lo último que vi”, aseguró Boutros.</p><p>El fiscal principal dijo que no tenía intención de culpar a su personal por la violación de la orden de sellado. Pero también dijo que había encontrado “consuelo” en Washington en una “posición de respaldo”.</p><p>La orden de McNally permitió la divulgación de la denuncia para “facilitar la aplicación de la ley penal”. Boutros argumentó en una presentación judicial el miércoles que uno de los propósitos de la conferencia de prensa era “disuadir futuros delitos” por parte del Tren de Aragua.</p><p>McNally no aceptó eso.</p><p>“No hubiera firmado una orden para la total discreción de toda la comunidad de aplicación de la ley para decidir que, en este momento, pensamos que lo que estamos haciendo aquí no debería ser sellado,” dijo McNally. “No hubiera concedido esa moción”.</p><p>Aunque McNally concluyó la audiencia sin dictar ninguna sanción, Boutros aún no está fuera de peligro. De hecho, audiencias similares podrían concretarse en múltiples casos pendientes. Por ejemplo, los miembros de los “Broadview Six” siguen pidiendo a la jueza Perry que designe a un abogado especial que investigue a Boutros y a otros en el Departamento de Justicia.</p><p>Mientras tanto, la jueza magistrada Keri Holleb Hotaling recientemente acordó un “breve” retraso de una audiencia durante la cual podría considerar sanciones contra las fuerzas del orden federales.</p><p>Holleb Hotaling dijo que realizará dicha audiencia después de que surgiera un video que <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/19/shooting-fbi-atf-hotaling-boutros-country-club-hills" target="_blank" >parecía contradecir</a> una declaración jurada que le habían dado. Ocurrió en el caso de tres personas acusadas en relación con el intento de robo de oficiales federales encubiertos en Country Club Hills.</p><p>Holleb Hotaling dio a los abogados defensores hasta el viernes para presentar un breve en el asunto pero no ha fijado una nueva fecha para la audiencia.</p><p>Finalmente, los abogados defensores del exdirector financiero del Hospital Loretto, Anosh Ahmed, siguen buscando una audiencia —o el despido permanente de cargos de fraude— sobre la mala conducta presunta por parte de un fiscal dentro de los procedimientos del gran jurado en ese caso.</p><p>La jueza de distrito Sharon Johnson Coleman ya ha amenazado con realizar una audiencia en ese asunto. La oficina de Boutros la evitó desestimando permanentemente los cargos contra dos de los coacusados de Ahmed.</p><p>Pero incluso mientras hacían eso, Coleman mandó al equipo de Boutros de regreso a la oficina con una advertencia.</p><p>“Asegúrate de que tu jefe entienda”, dijo Coleman, “que eso de la audiencia de evidencia sigue siendo una posibilidad. No estoy diciendo que eso se haya terminado, al menos en esta sala”.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (AI) y editado por </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a></p>

entries.title: Mayor Johnson finally explains his decision to bid $3.2B for parking meters before walking away
entries.summary: <p>Under fire from the City Council for hiding behind a non-disclosure agreement waived weeks ago, Mayor Brandon Johnson has finally come clean about why he offered $700 million more than a New York investment firm to re-acquire Chicago parking meters and about the financial risks that prompted his administration to abandon that $3.2 billion bid.</p><p>In a memo to Finance Committee members preparing for Monday’s showdown vote, Johnson's administration submitted an initial bid of $2.8 billion, advanced to the second round with a $2.85 billion bid and upped the ante to $3.2 billion after being told that nothing short of $3 billion stood a chance.</p><p>The higher bid also took into consideration the fact that the city’s acquisition was “expected to result in tax liabilities for the sellers” totaling “several hundred million dollars” that would not have accompanied an acquisition by a “private entity,” the memo states.</p><p>The city’s last, “best and final offer” was accepted as the initial winner. That allowed the Johnson administration to “evaluate the transaction on an exclusive basis and assess whether such a price and transaction structure was in the best interest” of Chicago taxpayers.</p><p>The Johnson administration ultimately concluded that the risk of undoing the parking meter deal that Chicagoans love to hate was not worth the reward either financially or politically.</p><p>To bankroll the massive “bond-financed” purchase, the city would have been required to issue debt backed by parking meter revenues at a time when Chicago is already saddled with a higher debt level per capita than any big city in the nation.</p><p>It would have been required to pledge to siphon other major sources of revenue that the city depends on “if parking habits shifted, alternative modes of transportation become more common” and “driver/commuter behaviors” changed.</p><p>That’s a distinct possibility amid a fast-changing landscape for parking demand that includes everything from self-driving vehicles and robot deliveries to congestion fees that discourage people from driving downtown.</p><p>“If parking meter revenue was not sufficient to cover the principal and interest payments, then spending on other infrastructure projects or critical services would have been impacted,” the mayor’s office memo states.</p><p>In order to attract “a large number of investors to a long-term borrowing of more than $3.2 billion” at what the mayor’s office called an “acceptable interest rate” would likely have required “pledging motor vehicle parking fine receipts as well as off-street parking/garage receipts in addition to all parking meter revenue, the memo states.</p><p>“Such supplemental revenue sources would serve as a backup repayment source in the event that parking system revenues were insufficient, thus putting the city’s current operating funds at risk,” the memo states.</p><p>The gap between annual revenue generated by the metered system after operating costs and debt service payments would have been “narrow throughout” the life of the bonds.</p><p>“The long-term expectations for driver behavior, system revenues and, more broadly, the city’s financial condition in those distant years is…the time period in which the greatest uncertainty exists,” the memo states.</p><p>“If those less-certain, longer-term revenues significantly under-performed, the system’s financial value would be greatly diminished…To the extent that parking meter revenues were not sufficient, the city’s general obligation bond ratings could have been negatively impacted…The risk of interest rates rising was a material concern.”</p><p>For all of those reasons and more, Johnson decided that the “most responsible decision was to walk away from the bid with no risk to the taxpayers and no penalty to the city,” the memo states.</p><p>That leaves the political hot potato created by Stonepeak’s $2.53 billion offer squarely in the City Council’s court.</p><p>The Council is facing a July 24 deadline to either authorize the sale to Stonepeak or reject it and risk a lawsuit by Chicago Parking Meters LLC, a consortium that includes Morgan Stanley, Allianz Capital Partners and the Sovereign Wealth Fund of Abu Dhabi.</p><p>Ald. Matt O'Shea (19th), one of Johnson's most outspoken City Council critics, said the mayor's after-the-fact explanation about a bid the city could not afford is an insult to a City Council he failed to consult.</p><p>"This is the equivalent of trying to explain with an apology weeks after you committed the original sin," O'Shea said Friday.</p><p>"People still don't trust him. When I say `people,' I'm talking about a majority of the City Council. And I would say the majority of taxpayers in our city don't trust him with the checkbook."</p><p>Asked if the mayor's memo would impact the City Council's vote, O'Shea said, "Not at all. The votes aren't there. The votes won't be there because people don't trust him."</p>

entries.title: Ex-Chicago ransomware negotiator gets nearly 6 years in prison for aiding hackers
entries.summary: <p>Former Chicago ransomware negotiator Angelo Martino was sentenced to nearly six years in federal prison for secretly helping cybercriminals extort clients he was hired to protect.</p><p>Martino, 41, was employed at the Chicago cybersecurity company DigitalMint, where he negotiated on behalf of companies whose computers were hacked and held with multimillion-dollar ransom payments.</p><p>But Martino helped orchestrate the same hacks that he was tasked with negotiating against. In all, he and his associates extorted more than $75 million in ransoms from four companies and a nonprofit organization that he represented as a negotiator.</p><p>The victims included hospitality, retail, medical and financial services businesses. Two of the ransom payoffs were for more than $25 million, according to court records.</p><p>The feds have seized $10 million of Martino’s properties in Florida and $10 million in his assets, including vehicles, a luxury fishing boat, a food truck and cryptocurrency.</p><p>Martino conspired with Kevin Martin, 36, another ransom threat negotiator for DigitalMint, and Ryan Clifford Goldberg, 41, an incident response manager for Sygnia Cybersecurity Services, according to prosecutors.</p><p>Goldberg’s role in the scheme was to identify computer weaknesses and gain access to victims’ networks. Martin’s job was to identify victims, extract data from their computers and lock their networks, prosecutors say. They were both sentenced earlier this year to four years in prison.</p><p>Another hearing to determine the amount of restitution Martino will be ordered to pay is scheduled for Sept. 17.</p><p>Martino and his associates began hacking into victims’ computer networks in 2023 using the software called ALPHV BlackCat.</p><p>BlackCat attackers paid Martino to provide confidential information about the negotiating position and strategy of his employer’s clients and enable the ransomware actors to maximize the payments by the victims, according to prosecutors.</p><p>In a previous statement, DigitalMint CEO Jonathan Solomon said the Justice Department informed the company of the allegations in April 2025, and Martino “was terminated the next day.”</p><p>Martin was also fired by DigitalMint, and Goldberg no longer works for Sygnia.</p><p>Cybersecurity crimes and cryptocurrency fraud have been on the rise in recent years.</p><p>Last year, more than $20 billion in losses to cybercrime were reported in the U.S., about a 26% increase from the prior year, according to prosecutors.</p>

entries.title: Indicted downstate Rep. Carol Ammons won’t step down: ‘I have done nothing wrong’
entries.summary: <p>An indicted central Illinois state representative will remain in office while fighting federal fraud charges for allegedly taking kickbacks on campaign expenses and angling state grant funding to organizations that hired her daughter.</p><p>Three days after a grand jury handed down <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/springfield/2026/07/08/carol-ammons-indicted-illinois-rep" target="_blank" ><u>a 10-count indictment</u></a> against state Rep. Carol Ammons, the six-term Urbana Democrat issued a written statement Friday asserting her innocence and her commitment to the job.</p><p>“I recognize that this news is deeply concerning to the people I have the privilege of serving, my supporters, my colleagues, and my community,” Ammons said. “Public service is built on trust, and I do not take that responsibility lightly.</p><p>“I want to be clear: I have done nothing wrong, and I strongly disagree with the allegations outlined in this indictment. I have complete confidence that the facts will demonstrate my innocence, and I intend to vigorously defend myself through the judicial process,” Ammons said.</p><p>Federal prosecutors say Ammons helped secure grant funding for a nonprofit that her daughter worked for until the House member was notified by state officials that it presented “an impermissible conflict of interest.”</p><p>Instead, Ammons helped other organizations that hired her daughter, “knowing full well it was a conflict of interest,” and netting the family more than $100,000 from 2017 to 2025, according to prosecutors.</p><p>Additionally, Ammons improperly paid family members out of her campaign fund, which also disbursed inflated payments to individuals who were expected “to provide cash kickbacks,” prosecutors said.</p><p>Ammons is unopposed in her bid for reelection this November in a race being overseen by her husband, Champaign County Clerk Aaron Ammons — who was charged in the same indictment with obstruction of justice for allegedly instructing a potential witness to “muddy the waters” for investigators. He’s up for reelection, too.</p><p>Rep. Ammons, who is scheduled for an initial court appearance next week, didn’t address her political future, but made clear she’s not going anywhere.</p><p>“I remain committed to serving the people of this district with integrity and transparency while this process moves forward,” Ammons said. “I ask for patience as the legal process unfolds, and I remain confident that the facts will ultimately speak for themselves.”</p><p>Illinois House Speaker Emanuel “Chris” Welch, D-Hillside, stripped Ammons of committee assignments and exiled her from House Democratic caucus meetings. </p><p>He called the allegations “extremely serious” but reiterated her right to due process — not enough for Republicans who are calling for her resignation and more stringent ethics reform in Springfield.</p><p>House Minority Leader Tony McCombie, R-Savanna, and members of her caucus filed a petition Friday to launch a special investigating committee on Ammons. </p><p>"The courts should absolutely do their job, but the Illinois House has a responsibility to do ours," McCombie said in a statement. "Accountability in the legislature cannot be outsourced to the criminal justice system."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure Benton still holds township post</b></h3><p>Rep. Ammons’ comments came a week after disgraced ex-state Rep. Harry Benton, D-Plainfield, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/07/06/harry-benton-investigation-report-misconduct-illinois-legislature" target="_blank" ><u>resigned from the Illinois House</u></a> amid unspecified sexual harassment allegations.</p><p>But Benton hasn’t given up his other elected post as the $72,000-per-year highway commissioner of far southwest suburban Wheatland Township, where trustees on Thursday unanimously passed a resolution urging him to step down.</p><p>“We believe the events of the past several months have significantly undermined public confidence in township government,” supervisor Michael Crowner said. “This request is not made as a judgment on facts that remain confidential, but in recognition that public service depends upon the confidence of the people we serve. We believe the residents of Wheatland Township deserve leadership that is free from questions that cannot presently be answered publicly.”</p><p>Township officials haven’t received any complaints about Benton, who had been banished from House Democratic caucus meetings for almost five months before the legislative inspector general submitted a report on Benton’s conduct to Welch, prompting the resignation.</p><p>Officials haven’t outlined the allegations against Benton, nor has he addressed them. The bipartisan Legislative Ethics Commission will decide whether to publicly release the report.<br></p>

entries.title: White Sox' Munetaka Murakami named American League All-Star reserve, will compete in Home Run Derby
entries.summary: <p>White Sox slugger Munetaka Murakami sure had an eventful Friday.</p><p>The Japanese slugger returned to the Sox lineup at first base and batting second against the Athletics, exactly six weeks after being sidelined by a Grade 2 right hamstring strain he suffered running out a grounder to first against Detroit on May 29.</p><p>Then the White Sox announced that Murakami, who entered with 20 home runs and 41 RBIs in his first 57 major league games, will be an American League All-Star reserve and participate in the Home Run Derby.</p><p>The news was leaked on the Rate Field video board with the words "Home Run Derby participant, Munetaka Murakami, Chicago White Sox All-Star." while the Sox took batting practice<br>The same message then appeared in the first inning and Sox confirmed the news with a tweet.</p><p>Murakami did not talk to reporters before the game.<br></p>

entries.title: Red Sox finally get to New York after 24-hour plane delay in Chicago
entries.summary: <p>NEW YORK — The Boston Red Sox, grounded for nearly 24 hours due to a pair of mechanical issues on their team plane, finally arrived at Citi Field on Friday afternoon, a little more than two hours before the scheduled first pitch of their series opener against the New York Mets.</p><p>The Red Sox got to the ballpark at 5:05 p.m. Eastern time, and the start of the game was pushed back by 35 minutes to 7:50 p.m.</p><p>"We're here," reliever Garrett Whitlock said, sitting in the dugout and sporting a tired smile.</p><p>The Red Sox expected to depart from Chicago on Thursday night, a few hours after they <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/07/09/red-sox-white-sox-patrick-sandoval-will-venable-andrew-benintendi-tanner-mcdougal-hagen-smith-shane-smith-scott-podsednik-alumni-home-run-derby-trevor-richards" >beat the White Sox 2-1</a> for their sixth straight win. But pitcher Peyton Tolle said the "tug" — which tows the planes around the runway — was malfunctioning.</p><p>The Red Sox remained on the tarmac until after midnight, at which point they went to a pair of hotels in Chicago. The team returned to the aircraft Friday morning but was delayed again by what interim manager Chad Tracy described as issues with "switches or light bulbs in the cockpit."</p><p>Center fielder Ceddanne Rafaela, whose addition to the AL All-Star team was announced over the plane loudspeaker by Tracy before the second delay, said players listened to music and played cards.</p><p>Tolle said he ate about five doughnuts Friday, though most of his teammates had burritos.</p><p>"We tried to make light of the situation, we tried to have fun with it," Tolle said. "But there was some frustration building, for sure.</p><p>"At one point, we kind of just looked at each other laughing because it was just ridiculous."</p><p>The Red Sox finally took off a little before 3 p.m. Eastern time and landed at LaGuardia Airport around 4:30 p.m. Team employees said the roughly two-mile drive to Citi Field was relatively easy during rush hour.</p><p>"Throw it back to travel ball days," Whitlock said. "Show and go. Go out there and play, have fun."</p><p>The Red Sox still planned to start Sonny Gray, who traveled with the team from Chicago.</p><p>"Nobody else you'd rather have start this baseball game than Sonny," Tolle said. "It's going to take a dog factor and Sonny has got that."</p><p>The delay was the second in two weeks for the Red Sox. Their flight from Denver to Boston turned around after half an hour on June 24 due to a mechanical issue.</p><p>The Red Sox didn't get home until around dawn on June 25 but beat the New York Yankees 6-3 hours later to start an 11-2 surge.</p><p>"I think it's some adversity for us," Rafaela said. "The message I sent to the guys was we have great momentum right now. That has to be our focus."<br></p>

entries.title: Chicago school board bars candidates from taking CPS vendors' campaign contributions
entries.summary: <p>The Board of Education is barring school board candidates from accepting campaign contributions from current or prospective Chicago Public Schools vendors to ward off conflicts or undue influence as election season forges ahead.</p><p>But questions remain about whether restrictions are too narrow as candidates collect millions in campaign cash ahead of an election that will determine who sits on the city’s first fully elected school board.</p><p>“As we enter into unprecedented waters for the board and campaigning, I thought it important that we inoculate the board from the optics of pay to play,” Board President Sean Harden said during discussion of the resolution at a June meeting.</p><p>The board approved the measure Wednesday in a 16-1 vote.</p><p>Each candidate would be responsible for confirming that campaign contributions aren’t coming from active CPS vendors or any organizations that have applied for district contracts, according to the resolution. The district relies on vendors for various goods and services, from landscaping to academic tools, whose contracts are approved by the board.</p><p>Nearly all current board members, half of whom were appointed by the mayor, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/05/26/51-candidates-are-running-for-chicagos-first-fully-elected-school-board" target="_blank" ><u>filed paperwork in May</u></a> to join the school board race as the governing body shifts from partially to fully elected next year. Many are facing challenges to their candidacies in the November election, and the process that determines if they'll appear on the ballot <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/06/04/half-of-chicago-school-board-candidates-are-facing-challenges-but-powerful-ctu-says-it-didnt-file-any" target="_blank" ><u>this fall is ongoing</u></a>.</p><p>Harden, who is not seeking to retain his seat, said the Better Government Association reviewed the resolution and told him it represented “the standard by which the board should be approaching this work.”</p><p>Bryan Zarou, BGA vice president of policy, called it a “step in the right direction” but noted the resolution was too narrowly targeted at vendors. For example, the resolution does not include language preventing individuals connected with vendors from making personal contributions.</p><p>“There still needs to be a lot more work to really tighten those loopholes that exist,” Zarou said in an interview.</p><p>Verjeana McCotter-Jacobs, CEO of the National School Board Association, said it's common for large elected school boards to pass such resolutions.</p><p>“It's definitely for the public, but it should also raise the opportunity for board members to think about their donations,” McCotter-Jacobs said.</p><p>Campaign finance records show that board members Che “Rhymefest” Smith and Jessica Biggs both recently received campaign contributions from law firm Cozen O’Connor, which has a contract with the board. Cozen O’Connor has represented the Board of Education in a lawsuit filed by former CPS CEO Pedro Martinez over the decision to fire him.</p><p>Disclosures also show that Anthony Fiore, vice president of Open Kitchens, <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/curious-city/2025/08/13/school-lunch-used-to-pass-the-test" target="_blank" ><u>which has a contract to provide meals</u></a> for CPS, has contributed to the campaign funds of members Carlos Rivas, Ellen Rosenfeld, Jessica Biggs and Therese Boyle.</p><p>The resolution states that board members who accepted donations from a vendor before adoption of the resolution should either recuse themselves from voting for agenda items involving those vendors or return the donation and notify the district and its ethics officer. But it is unclear if that applies to Fiore’s contribution because it was a personal donation.</p><p>Rivas said he will consult with his attorney on how to proceed.</p><p>“Common practice before the resolution was recusal, and I suspect that will continue to be the case for all board members to avoid actual or perceived conflicts,” Rivas said in a text message.</p><p>Biggs, Boyle, Smith and Rosenfeld didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.</p><p>The board passed the resolution without much discussion. But during a meeting in June, several board members questioned whether it should extend to donations from the district's labor unions since the board also votes on their contracts.</p><p>The Chicago Teachers Union <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/graphics/education/2024/school-board-finance-tracker/" target="_blank" ><u>was a big spender during the 2024</u></a> election when only half of the school board seats were up for grabs. The union’s two political action committees shelled out <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/chicago-school-board/2024/11/05/first-ever-elections-cps-power-dynamics" target="_blank" ><u>$4.3 million on those races</u></a>, according to an analysis by Chalkbeat Chicago.</p><p>Charter schools interests and groups that <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/chicago-school-board/2024/10/03/emboldened-by-cps-strife-ctu-critics-pour-more-cash-into-school-board-elections" target="_blank" ><u>are critical of the union</u></a> also ponied up $3.5 million during the historic elections through two key super PACs. That included the INCS Action Committee, affiliated with the Illinois Network of Charter Schools, and the Urban Center, which <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/chicago-school-board/2024/09/06/chicago-school-board-elections-see-big-school-choice-cash-including-from-billionaires" target="_blank" ><u>were bolstered by millionaires and billionaires.</u></a> The board also votes on charter school contracts.</p><p>Spending in this year's elections <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-school-board/2026/02/19/big-money-expected-to-flow-in-novembers-historic-chicago-school-board-race" target="_blank" ><u>is expected to surpass 2024</u></a> as the entire 21-member board is up for a vote, more than the 10 seats up for election that year. More than $13 million was spent during the 2024 campaign season, according to the Chalkbeat analysis, with 31 candidates on the ballot.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/05/26/51-candidates-are-running-for-chicagos-first-fully-elected-school-board" target="_blank" ><u>Fifty-one people have entered the race</u></a> this year, but that number is likely to dwindle after the ballot challenge process concludes. Candidate campaign committees have already received more than $2 million in contributions. Campaigns file their latest financial disclosures next week.</p><p>There are already <a class="Link" href="https://www.cps.edu/sites/cps-policy-rules/policies/500/503/503-1/" target="_blank" ><u>disclosure policies in place for board members</u></a>. They are required to check every month for conflicts of interest and must recuse themselves from voting on matters involving contracts with entities they have economic interests in, according to CPS policy.</p>

entries.title: Pitchfork Festivals sues co-founder, claiming $564k in funds were misappropriated
entries.summary: <p>The company behind the now-shuttered Pitchfork Music Festival is suing its co-founder, alleging he misappropriated more than $500,000 in festival funds.</p><p>Pitchfork Festivals LLC filed a lawsuit Monday in federal court in Chicago accusing co-founder Mike Reed of keeping $564,680 by falsely claiming the money reimbursed expenses he had already acquired while preparing for the 2025 festival before it was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/music/2024/11/11/pitchfork-music-festival-wont-return-in-2025" target="_blank" >canceled</a>.</p><p>Pitchfork Music Festival, which ran for 19 years at Union Park, was canceled in 2024 after organizers said the rapidly evolving music festival landscape was behind the decision to end the event.</p><p>Pitchfork and Big Stik LLC, Reed’s event production company, entered into contract in 2019 to provide production services for the music festival, including maintaining an event bank account.</p><p>The lawsuit claims that Pitchfork advanced $3,970,180 to Big Stik in preparation for the 2024 festival.</p><p>Within 30 days of the 2024 festival’s conclusion, Pitchfork’s head of procurement, Alys Wood-Bibby, emailed Reed stating that Condé Nast — Pitchfork’s New York-based parent company — planned to move forward with the festival in 2025. However, according to the complaint, the parties never established a “scope of work” agreement, and Reed did not submit any budget or expense requests related to 2025 planning activities.</p><p>The complaint further alleges that Reed did not raise any claims, objections or notices regarding “wind-down” costs after being informed that the 2025 festival would not move forward.</p><p>Reed was notified the 2025 festival was canceled on Nov. 11, 2024, according to the lawsuit.</p><p>On Jan. 8, 2025, Pitchfork asked Big Stik to return the remaining money in Pitchfork's event account. Big Stik refused and allegedly submitted a fabricated "Wind Down Settlement Report" to Pitchfork's finance director the next day that contained material misrepresentations designed to account for the exact amount Pitchfork was seeking to recover.</p><p>Reed wrote that “the remaining monies are incurred and attributed to the canceled 2025 event and the wind-down of all operations.” However, the lawsuit alleges that “a large portion of the costs” had not been incurred as of Jan. 9, 2025, and accuses Reed of falsely attributing $565,680 to expenses related to labor, production and cancellation fees, storage, legal services, accounting and taxes.</p><p>The lawsuit alleges that Reed reverse engineered the precise balance remaining in Pitchfork’s event account.</p><p>Instead of returning the funds, Reed allegedly transferred the money from the company contracted by Pitchfork to another entity under his control, At Pluto Ltd,</p><p>The lawsuit alleges that Reed concealed the transfer of funds and that Pitchfork only discovered it through the discovery process in a related arbitration proceeding.</p><p>Neither Reed nor Condé Nast responded to a request for comment.</p><p>Pitchfork accused Reed of fraud, unjust enrichment, breach of fiduciary duty, conversion, accounting and fraudulent transfer.</p><p>Reed has been a fixture in Chicago’s music scene for more than 20 years. In a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2023/10/24/23928437/mike-reed-pitchfork-music-festival-separatist-party-hungry-brain-constellation" target="_blank" >2024 interview with the Sun-Times</a>, Reed described Pitchfork Music Festival as “an event for people who are really into music.” He said the festival stood in contrast to larger events like Lollapalooza and Windy City Smokeout, which he characterized as “lifestyle events.”</p><p>According to Reed, music was the primary draw for Pitchfork attendees, while people attending “lifestyle” events were often seeking a broader experience. </p><p>Reed also owns local venues Constellation and the Hungry Brain.<br></p>
